29 October 2008

## Circular to All Licensed Corporations and Registered Institutions Regarding Supervision and Risk Management

This circular reminds the senior management of all licensed corporations and registered institutions of the need to maintain good practices in supervision and risk management.

The Code of Conduct 1 and Internal Control Guidelines 2 issued by the Commission provide guidance to persons licensed by or registered with the Securities and Futures Commission on the standards and conduct reasonably expected of them in order to protect their business operations, their clients and other intermediaries from financial loss arising from theft, fraud, other dishonest acts, professional misconduct or omissions.

In view of recent developments, where certain key risk areas have come to light, senior management are reminded to maintain adequate oversight in the following 3 key areas in particular.

## Senior management responsibility

Firms are expected to maintain effective control procedures to prevent errors, omissions, fraud and other unauthorized activities.  In particular, senior management of firms with business lines undergoing rapid growth should assess whether or not adequate resources have been allocated to support and control functions to ensure that they are commensurate with such business growth.

Senior management of each firm should enhance their staff's awareness of the potential risks inherent in the firm's operations in the context of the functions performed by such staff. Support and control functions should be performed by qualified and experienced individuals who have sufficient understanding of their role and responsibility in identifying any violation of internal or external requirements as well as in being vigilant regarding any suspicious activities, transactions or product valuations.

All supervisory staff should have sufficient skill and authority to perform such functions. Senior management must take timely remedial action against any non-compliance or suspicious issues identified by the control systems.

## Trading controls

Appropriate trading limits and position limits should be established and monitored at appropriate intervals.  Consideration should be given to having limits on individual trades of significant size and cumulative gross nominal exposure, in addition to limits on net exposure. Trader confirmations should be sent out and reconciled promptly by back-office staff independent of front office.

For firms that carry out proprietary trading or market making, it is a good practice to put in place a trading mandate for each trader to define the products, markets and strategies authorized for the trader.   Likewise, firms should reconcile margin or collateral requirements to trader or book level. There should also be a regular review of the records of individual traders and trading units and the profit and loss attribution of the trading operations to ensure unusual items are properly analyzed and understood in the context of the trader's strategy and positions.

## Red flag transactions reporting

Firms should consider implementing a systematic process for handling 'red flag' transactions reported by staff. Red flag transactions would include unusually large trading volumes, an unusual amount of profit and loss attributable to a trader vis-à-vis his trading strategy, transactions with no legitimate purpose or a recurring pattern of late allocations, errors or cancellations and questionable product valuations.

To enable the above process to function properly, a clear reporting channel for red flag transactions should be put in place to ensure that staff can report any suspicious transactions swiftly to the appropriate level in the firm where decisions on corrective action can be taken.

It should be noted that the above risk areas are by no means exhaustive. Each intermediary should review its own circumstances and ensure that appropriate risk management and internal controls are put in place and effectively enforced.
